exposureStatement: Read only the frozen blind question/options/citations packet and actual source text/pixels; author batch and author scripts not opened. Independent answers and observations are persisted before revealing author keys.

sourceVisualObservations.notes: Printed 1. Lecture Number 7, Manipulator Kinematics, title and institutional marks only.

Printed 2. Objectives include DOF, homogeneous transformations, DH, FK, PUMA 560 and differential drive. The later lecture may not actually contain the promised PUMA worked example; objectives are not treated as proof of that coverage.
Printed 3. Four-part outline: introduction, DH parameters, FK and differential drive. Administrative outline only.
Printed 4. Text contrasts rigid-link joint-chain manipulators with differential-drive robots whose wheel velocities control motion. No additional mechanical diagram.

Printed 5. Kinematics studies motion without its causing forces, includes time derivatives, and assigns frames to links to track articulation. Lower-right box is blank, not a missing technical figure inferred from extraction.

Printed 6. FK applications: joint-command Cartesian observations, demonstration joint-to-task-space mapping, collision geometry, differentiable optimization and named simulator examples. Broad implementation claims are survey motivations rather than universal product-version guarantees.

Printed 7. Independent configuration variables define manipulator DOF. Rigid spatial body has three translations and three rotations. Revolute and prismatic each contribute one independent freedom in the stated serial-manipulator context.

Printed 8. Neighboring rigid links are connected by constraining joints; revolute rotation and prismatic translation about/along fixed axes. Numbering starts at fixed link 0, first moving link 1, free end n. Five/six-joint prevalence is a broad source remark, not a new census.

Printed 9. Six actual mechanism drawings: pin hinge, keyed prismatic shaft, cylindrical sleeve, planar block, threaded screw and ball-and-socket. Labels give R1, P1, screw1, cylindrical2, planar3, spherical3. Screw marked R is incomplete shorthand; fixed-lead coupling makes one independent variable.
Printed 10. DH parameters a, alpha, d and theta; systematic frame assignment and geometry-to-matrix model. No uniqueness or universal reachability guarantee appears.
Printed 11. Curved physical link between axes i−1 and i; a_(i−1) is the straight segment with right-angle marks at both axes, not material-path length. Alpha_(i−1) denotes twist between axes.
Printed 12. The neighboring link sketch shows offset d_i along axis i and joint angle theta_i between the common-normal directions. The text identifies d and theta as connection parameters.

Printed 13. Table defines a_i as Z_i-to-Z_(i+1) distance along X_i, alpha_i as their angle about X_i, d_i as X_(i−1)-to-X_i distance along Z_i, and theta_i as their angle about Z_i. The side sketch labels preceding geometry a_(i−1), alpha_(i−1), so indices must be retained rather than conflated.

Printed 14. Actual factor order is Rx(alpha_(i−1)) Dx(a_(i−1)) Rz(theta_i) Dz(d_i). The expanded third-row second entry visibly reads sin(alpha_i), inconsistent with multiplying the factors, which gives sin(alpha_(i−1)) cos(theta_i). Translation column is a, −d sin(alpha), d cos(alpha). Prose direction wording differs from the usual coordinate-map interpretation of the superscript/subscript notation; questions should declare their convention.

Printed 15. Six frame-assignment steps: common perpendicular/intersection of axes i and i+1; origin on axis i; z_i along joint axis; x_i along common normal or normal to the plane of intersecting axes; y_i right-handed; boundary-frame choices simplify parameters. Intersecting noncollinear axes have a defined plane; parallel normals can be nonunique.

Printed 16. Planar 3R arm diagram and table: rows (alpha,a,d,theta) are (0,0,0,theta1), (0,L1,0,theta2), (0,L2,0,theta3). Frame 3 origin is at the final revolute axis, not an unspecified distal tool point. Parallel axes and chosen coplanar frames yield zero twist/offset.

Printed 17. Three homogeneous factors multiply in order T01 T12 T23. Result rotation uses theta123; translation is (L1 cos(theta1)+L2 cos(theta12), L1 sin(theta1)+L2 sin(theta12), 0). The origin position contains no theta3, but an offset point on link 3 can depend on its orientation.

Printed 18. RPR diagram shows first/third rotation and middle prismatic extension. Table has alpha1=90 degrees, theta2=0, d2 variable, d3=L2 constant. Separate mechanical sketch labels L1/L2/L3, but the stated transform/table uses its chosen frame locations, not an assumed world-floor/tool-tip pose.

Printed 19. RPR factors visibly give Rz(theta1), then Rx(90°) with translation (0,−d2,0), then Rz(theta3) with z translation L2. Expanded row 2 column 3 prints −cos(theta3), but factor multiplication gives −cos(theta1). Translation is ((L2+d2)sin(theta1),−(L2+d2)cos(theta1),0).

Printed 20. Planar body diagram shows heading phi from world +x, axle midpoint (x,y), and d from midpoint to a wheel. Text explicitly defines full wheel separation 2d, common wheel radius r, and wheel linear speeds v_l=r u_l, v_r=r u_r.

Printed 21. Table gives equal wheel speeds straight, right greater than left left-turn, reverse inequality right-turn, and v_r=−v_l unconditionally clockwise. The last sign claim is incomplete; the equations on printed 23 determine sign from v_r−v_l. Zero opposite speeds also give rest. Applications include service/navigation/warehouse.

Printed 22. Planar pose is (x,y,phi). Mapping goes wheel velocities to body velocity to pose change. Stated advantages are simple axle drive and in-place maneuverability; no physics/torque dynamics are supplied.

Printed 23. v=(v_r+v_l)/2 and omega=(v_r−v_l)/(2d), with v_wheel=r u_wheel. World rates are xdot=v cos(phi), ydot=v sin(phi), phidot=omega. The displayed matrix output order is (phidot,xdot,ydot), input order (u_l,u_r), and first row (−r/(2d),+r/(2d)).

Printed 24. Summary repeats DH, FK and differential drive. Six-joint sentence needs the one-DOF/local full-rank/task-scope qualification; joint count alone does not guarantee all poses, uniqueness or absence of singularities.
Printed 25. Two reference entries only: Craig and Merzouki/Samantaray/Pathak/Bouamama. No new technical equation or mechanism.
Printed 26. Thank You courtesy only.

answers.reasoning: The introduction explicitly separates a rigid-link joint chain from a mobile differential-drive system controlled by wheel velocities.
Link-attached frames move as the mechanism articulates. Kinematics describes that geometry, not the forces or torques causing motion.
Joint configurations are inputs and Cartesian tool poses are outputs, so this is forward rather than inverse kinematics.
The stated FK role maps joint-configuration commands into Cartesian observations; it does not optimize the policy or replace a torque model.

The source lists collision geometry, differentiable trajectory optimization and link geometry inside simulators. It calls FK relevant to sim-to-real but does not guarantee successful transfer with no mismatch.
Configuration DOF counts independent joint coordinates, not matrix entries or merely three position coordinates.
An unconstrained spatial rigid-body pose has three translational plus three rotational freedoms; the planar 2+1 alternative describes a different task space.
A revolute joint permits rotation about its fixed axis; a prismatic joint permits translation along its fixed axis. Each has one independent coordinate here.
The slide numbers the immobile base 0, the first moving link 1 and the free-end link n.
A joint connects links while restricting allowable relative motion. It neither releases all constraints nor fixes every joint against all motion.
The definition is direct surface contact between the two bodies; point-only contact is not the lower-pair definition supplied.
The visible labels give cylindrical P+R two freedoms, planar P-P-R three, and spherical R-R-R three.
For the explicitly assumed fixed-lead screw, axial displacement is determined by rotation; the two visible kinds of motion are coupled, unlike the independent cylindrical P+R coordinates.
The planar block can translate twice and rotate once; the ball-and-socket has three rotations. These are the pictured three-freedom mechanisms.
The four named parameters are link length a, twist alpha, offset d and joint angle theta.
DH systematically assigns frames and derives serial-link transforms. It is not a claim that inverse kinematics is unique or all poses reachable.
A rigid link fixes the relationship between its supported axes through their common-normal distance a and twist alpha.
The straight a_(i−1) line has perpendicular markers at both joint axes. It is not the curved body length or base-to-tool reach.
The displayed connection description names d and theta; a and alpha describe the link’s supported-axis geometry instead.
The table explicitly defines a_i along X_i and alpha_i about X_i. One is a length and the other an angle.
d_i is the separation of the X_(i−1) and X_i common-normal directions measured along Z_i; theta_i is their relative rotation about Z_i.
The frame-i to frame-(i−1) matrix uses preceding-link geometry a_(i−1), alpha_(i−1), together with current d_i and theta_i. The table’s generic link index is not a reason to replace all indices by i.
The visible factorization is Rx(alpha_(i−1)) Dx(a_(i−1)) Rz(theta_i) Dz(d_i). Reordering the x- and z-axis operations generally changes the result.
Dx contributes (a,0,0); the final z translation is rotated by Rx into (0,−d sin(alpha),d cos(alpha)). Rz does not change its own z-axis direction. Sum gives (a,−d sin(alpha),d cos(alpha)).
Row 3 of Rx is (0,sin(alpha),cos(alpha)); column 2 of Rz is (−sin(theta),cos(theta),0). Their dot product is sin(alpha) cos(theta), with alpha=alpha_(i−1), not the printed sin(alpha_i).
With sin(90°)=1 and cos(90°)=0, translation (a,−d sin(alpha),d cos(alpha)) becomes (2,−3,0) metres.
Step 3 assigns z_i along the i-th joint axis; x_i follows the common-normal construction instead.

The stated construction chooses a common perpendicular and puts the origin at its meeting with axis i. It does not use the material midpoint or tool tip. For parallel axes a choice may be nonunique, but the instruction remains a valid construction.
For the explicitly noncollinear intersecting axes, x_i is normal to their plane. Then y_i completes the right-handed frame; zero common-normal length does not eliminate an axis.
Step 6 matches frame 0 to frame 1 at zero first joint variable, then chooses terminal origin/x direction to make parameters simple, often zero.
Row 2 is alpha1=0, a1=L1, d2=0, theta2 variable. L2 belongs to the next link-geometry row.
The shown axes are parallel and chosen frames have no out-of-plane displacement. Zero alpha/d does not force zero link lengths or zero joint angles.
Reading the product: translation uses first-link theta1 and second-link theta12; final rotation accumulates theta123.
The translation column has no theta3, so the frame-3 origin stays fixed when only theta3 changes. The rotation block changes; an offset tool point need not stay fixed.
theta12=90°−90°=0° and theta123=30°. Position is (2 cos90°+1 cos0°,2 sin90°+1 sin0°,0)=(1,2,0) m, orientation 30°.
Rotate the local offset (1,0) by +90° to (0,1), then add the frame origin (3,0). The tool is (3,1) m, not the unrotated offset (4,0).
The table’s first and third revolute joints vary theta1/theta3, while the middle prismatic joint varies d2. The remaining listed geometry is constant.
The visible second row fixes alpha1 at 90 degrees and theta2 at zero; third-row d3 is L2, not the variable d2.
The middle translation is (0,−d2,0); its rotated z direction sends L2 along the same negative-y direction before Rz(theta1). Rotating (0,−(L2+d2),0) gives ((L2+d2)sin(theta1),−(L2+d2)cos(theta1),0).
The final local z column after Rx(90°) is (0,−1,0). Rz(theta1) maps it to (sin(theta1),−cos(theta1),0), independent of theta3. The printed −cos(theta3) is inconsistent.
Substituting theta1=0 and theta3=90° into the erroneous column gives (0,0,0). A rotation matrix column must have norm one, so this cannot be valid.
L2+d2=0.6+0.4=1 m. At theta1=90°, sin=1 and cos=0, giving (1,0,0) m.
The prose explicitly gives common wheel radius r and full separation 2d; the diagram’s d marker is only midpoint-to-wheel half-separation.
Rolling linear speed is angular rate times radius: v_r=r u_r. Dimensions are metres times radians/second, giving metres/second with radians dimensionless.
Equal speeds make the yaw numerator v_r−v_l zero. Their average is the shared speed, producing straight translation if nonzero and rest if zero.
For d>0, omega=(v_r−v_l)/(2d) has the positive sign of the stated difference. The question correctly asks yaw sign rather than conflating that with reversing-path language.
With v_l=−v_r, v=0 and omega=v_r/d. Thus clockwise requires v_r<0, counterclockwise requires v_r>0, and both zero give rest; opposite-speed equality alone does not establish clockwise rotation.
The planar body pose includes two position coordinates and heading: x,y,phi. Wheel rates are inputs, not the pose itself.
The source maps wheel rates through body forward/yaw velocity into world-frame pose derivatives.
Midpoint forward speed is the average (v_r+v_l)/2 and yaw is the difference divided by full track width 2d.
Wheel linear speeds are 0.2 and 0.4 m/s. Their average is 0.30 m/s; difference 0.20 divided by 0.50 m gives +0.40 rad/s.
At phi=90°, cos=0 and sin=1. In the explicitly requested xdot,ydot,phidot order, the rates are (0,0.30,0.40), with mixed translational/angular units.
The actual matrix places phidot first, then xdot and ydot. This differs from the common x,y,phi pose-list order and from question 52’s explicitly requested order.
Input order left then right gives omega=−r u_l/(2d)+r u_r/(2d), hence row [−r/(2d),+r/(2d)].
Holding wheel linear speeds fixed leaves their average unchanged. Doubling full separation doubles the yaw denominator and halves omega.
Both v=r(u_r+u_l)/2 and omega=r(u_r−u_l)/(2d) are linear in common radius when wheel angular rates and d are fixed. Each scales by two, including zero-rate limits.
Add/subtract the forward and yaw equations: r u_r=v+d omega and r u_l=v−d omega. Divide by r to recover the two angular commands.
Wheel speeds are −0.3 and +0.3 m/s, average zero. Difference 0.6 over separation 0.5 gives +1.2 rad/s, so the robot rotates counterclockwise in place.
Substitute xdot=v cos(phi), ydot=v sin(phi): −v cos(phi)sin(phi)+v sin(phi)cos(phi)=0. The forward component instead equals v; unequal wheel speeds can still give nonzero yaw.

General spatial pose has six local freedoms, and six independent one-DOF joints can supply them at a full-rank nonsingular configuration. Count alone does not guarantee global reachability, unique inverse kinematics, or a need for six freedoms in every simpler task.
